newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader warns Russia not to weaken treaty.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader warns Russia not to weaken treaty.

text.p: Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko warned Russia on Tuesday against watering down the Union Treaty he signed with President Boris Yeltsin last month.

But at the same time Lukashenko, whose authoritarian style and scarcely reformed Soviet-style economy prompted alarmed Kremlin liberals to drastically trim the treaty, asserted the former Soviet republic's independence.

Russian liberals, led by First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, headed off what they saw as a bid by conservatives to bind Yeltsin to union with Minsk by filleting the treaty signed on April 2 by Yeltsin and Lukashenko.
Details of the union were sliced out and contained in a separate "charter", which the two presidents initialled but, at Russia's insistence, delayed signing to allow "public debate".
The month allowed for this discussion -- which was decidedly low-key -- has now expired and officials have indicated the charter may be signed toward the end of May.
Apparently still concerned that Chubais and his allies might try to reduce the scope of the vaguely worded charter, Lukashenko said he opposed any changes in the original document.

"What more can be put in it? One president's disagreements cannot be put in the charter," he told reporters. "The charter was initialled by two presidents, even though that's nonsense. Civil servants initial things. It is effectively signed."

Lukashenko said the discussions in Russian media about the lengthy charter, which the brief treaty described as "an inalienable part" of the treaty, had "inflicted irreparable damage" and dampened Russian public support for the union.
Integration is popular in communist and nationalist circles, where many people favour recreating the Soviet Union.
But Russian television channels have dwelt on the dangers for Russia of elevating the hardline conservative Lukashenko to a shared presidency with Yeltsin.
Lukashenko said an opinion poll had shown Russian support for integration with Belarus had fallen to 62 percent from 90 percent. He gave no other details of the survey.
In an apparent dig at Chubais, Lukashenko said of Yeltsin's advisers: "They should show a bit more humility. The decisions will be taken by the presidents of Belarus and Russia."
Responding to criticism of his crackdown on opponents who took to the streets in protest at the union treaty, the Belarus leader said he would not respond to pressure from abroad.

"We're a state too, like the United States. We are founder members of the United Nations," he said, pledging to follow "independent policies" in relation to Russia, the states of the European Union and other countries.
